content: This is a core obligation under the right to health, as outlined in international human rights frameworks. Essential medicines, as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO), must be made available to meet the minimum essential levels of health care. The right to health encompasses access to a variety of facilities, goods, services, and conditions necessary to achieve the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health. This includes ensuring access to sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services, which must be provided equitably and without discrimination. Access to SRH information, including details on safe abortion and post-abortion care, must be provided in accessible formats. Criminalizing abortion or imposing barriers such as mandatory waiting periods, third-party consent, or judicial authorization constitutes discrimination and violates the right to health and equality. States must take steps to reduce maternal mortality and morbidity, particularly by addressing unsafe abortions. This includes ensuring access to safe, legal, and effective abortion services where the life or health of the pregnant individual is at risk, or where carrying a pregnancy to term would cause substantial pain or suffering, such as in cases of rape or non-viable pregnancies. Women in rural areas, who face disproportionately high maternal mortality rates, must have access to affordable and comprehensive SRH services. Such care must not be used as evidence in legal proceedings against women or abortion care providers. States must repeal laws and policies that create barriers to SRH services, including those that criminalize abortion, impose biased counseling requirements, or mandate waiting periods. Restrictive abortion laws and practices that deny life-saving medical care or force women to seek unsafe abortions violate the right to life and may constitute gender-based violence or arbitrary killings. Access to SRH services, including safe abortion, must be confidential, non-judgmental, and respectful of privacy. Laws and policies must be evidence-based, proportionate, and aligned with international human rights standards to protect the health, dignity, and rights of all individuals.
